overview: This record represents modern Greenland, whose 1960 map start comes after its 1953 incorporation into the Danish kingdom. Greenland later gained Home Rule and then expanded self-government. Inuit communities, language and knowledge remain central to a society with both towns and smaller settlements.

periods.title: Integration and rapid social change
periods.summary: New housing, schools and industries developed under policies largely directed from Denmark.

periods.title: Home Rule
periods.summary: Greenland obtained its own elected governing institutions under the Home Rule arrangement.

periods.title: Self-government
periods.summary: A new arrangement expanded Greenland’s authority and recognized its people’s right to self-determination.

sections.title: A living landscape with a long history

items.text: The Aasivissuit to Nipisat landscape preserves thousands of years of hunting and settlement. Large communal winter houses and inland caribou hunting features record organized work and shared living. The remains belong to several successive cultures, extending far earlier than this modern map record.

Caribou hunting used hides and drive systems, while coastal waters supplied fish and marine animals. Routes connected sea, fjords and interior across the seasons. Some hunting journeys still follow this broad pattern, linking present families with knowledge preserved in the landscape.

The national museum displays kayaks, open skin boats called umiaq, and dogsleds. Their forms were adapted to Arctic travel and hunting conditions. These were specialized technologies refined through experience, as carefully suited to their tasks as a modern vehicle.

One museum umiaq was still working in West Greenland until 1966. That date makes a useful surprise: skin boats belong to recent family memories as well as ancient history. The museum records continuing kayak and sled use especially in the north.

From the 1950s, housing schemes promoted larger new dwellings; later investment concentrated in open-water towns. Concrete apartment buildings accommodated newcomers, but housing shortages persisted. Decisions about where services were funded also encouraged families to leave smaller settlements.

Education reforms increasingly emphasized Danish. Between 1961 and 1976, more than 1,500 pupils went to Denmark after sixth grade, living with foster families. Such schooling offered qualifications but also separated children from familiar language, relatives and home surroundings.

Queen Ingrid’s Sanatorium opened in Nuuk in 1954 with 211 beds for tuberculosis patients. By 1962, the improved situation allowed it also to serve as a general hospital. This was a major change in access to treatment, although tuberculosis was not permanently eliminated.

Between 1955 and 1971, the specially built tuberculosis ship Misigssût travelled the coast to inhabited places. A visiting medical ship helped reach communities separated by sea and enormous distances. Public health needed a transport plan as much as a building.

In drum dancing, a performer moves a qilaat drum and strikes its frame with a stick. Songs can concern hunting, affection, longing or humour. These living performances share stories of ordinary life at celebrations and gatherings, rather than treating heritage as silent museum objects.

Historically, song duels could channel quarrels into performances that teased or mocked an opponent. Audience laughter helped decide the contest. The Greenlandic heritage inventory describes this as a way to reduce conflict, an argument with rhythm and an audience.

Section 20 of the 2009 law reads in Kalaallisut: “Kalaallit oqaasii tassaapput Kalaallit Nunaanni pisortatigoortumik oqaatsit.” Translation: “Greenlandic is the official language in Greenland.” This is an attested modern legal sentence, written with Latin letters, rather than a reconstructed ancient phrase.

The 2008 referendum supported expanded self-government, which began in June 2009. Greenland’s elected Inatsisartut and its government, Naalakkersuisut, make decisions in transferred fields. This history concerns Greenlanders seeking greater authority over their own lives and institutions.

ending.text: Greenland continues as a self-governing part of the Danish realm. The 2009 framework recognizes a right to self-determination and provides a process for possible independence. This is an ongoing society, not a civilization that ended in 1960.
